query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating high-throughput DSC measurements with third‐generation CALPHAD thermodynamic modeling will enable accurate and efficient determination of melting temperature, latent heat (enthalpy of fusion), entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a broad range of high‐entropy alloys. This synergy leverages the chemical short‐range order effect arising from multicomponent mixing.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, single-phase high-entropy alloy solid solutions (e.g., FCC, BCC, or mixed structures) with minimal contamination and controlled chemical homogeneity.
generation.intervention: Perform standardized high-throughput DSC experiments over extended temperature ranges with careful control near melting and combine the results with advanced CALPHAD modeling that incorporates improved Gibbs energy descriptions accounting for configurational entropy, thermal vacancy effects, and local chemical ordering. Complement DSC with in situ techniques such as dilatometry or high-temperature X-ray diffraction to capture volume changes.
generation.conditions: Experiments are conducted under controlled atmospheres (inert or vacuum) to prevent oxidation; heating rates are standardized for direct comparison; the method is applied to high-entropy alloys with diverse crystal structures and compositions in the regime where a single solid solution is expected.
generation.structural_mediator: The interplay between high configurational entropy and local chemical ordering (or emerging short-range order) governs phase stability and influences the enthalpy and entropy contributions at melting.
generation.mechanism: DSC experiments provide precise heat capacity curves near the melting point whose integration yields the enthalpy and entropy of fusion. CALPHAD modeling, using third-generation thermodynamic descriptions, accounts for thermal vacancy concentrations and deviations from a random solid-solution behavior. This combination ties experimental observations to physical models that predict liquid-phase thermodynamics and the associated volume change at melting.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated approach will predict melting temperatures within ±2–5% of independent benchmark techniques, and it will yield latent heat, entropy of fusion, and volume change data with similar accuracy. Trends across different alloy systems (FCC vs. BCC HEAs) will be systematically captured.
generation.baseline: Traditional methods relying solely on DSC analysis with simple rule-of-mixture or second-generation CALPHAD models have shown larger errors (≈10% or more) and less reliable predictions across varied HEA compositions.
generation.boundary: The approach may be less applicable for systems exhibiting strong elemental segregation, multi-phase melting, or extremely rapid solidification kinetics, where local inhomogeneities or oxidation effects could distort DSC signals and thermodynamic predictions.
generation.uncertainty: Residual uncertainties may arise from calibration issues in DSC, potential limitations in existing thermodynamic databases for novel HEA compositions, and the experimental challenge of accurately measuring volume changes at very high temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative set of high-entropy alloys covering diverse crystal structures and compositions. For each alloy, perform DSC measurements under identical, controlled conditions to obtain Cp(T) curves near melting, and measure volume changes using in-situ dilatometry or high-temperature XRD. Independently, use drop calorimetry or another complementary calorimetric method to directly determine melting temperature and enthalpy of fusion. Compare these results to the predictions obtained from the integrated DSC + CALPHAD approach.
measurements: Melting temperature from DSC and independent drop calorimetry
Enthalpy of fusion by integrating DSC heat capacity data
Entropy of fusion via Cp/T integration
Volume change at melting from in-situ dilatometry or high-temperature XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, for multiple high-entropy alloys, the integrated approach yields melting temperatures, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, or volume change values that differ by more than ±5% from the independently measured benchmarks, the hypothesis is falsified.

He critically reviewed all relevant experimental data available before 2006 and evaluated missing fusion enthalpies values based on measured enthalpy of fusion and volume change on melting for Y2O3. Zinkevich [] database for rare earth sesquioxides is openly available at the NIST website [] and was used in this work without any modifications. cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1. The Third-Generation Gibbs Energy Expressions for Pure Cr and V
cited_evidence.text: The reliable thermodynamic properties of pure Cr and V are the essential inputs to establish their Gibbs energy expressions. Recently, the measured thermodynamic properties including heat capacity (Cp), heat content (HT–H298), enthalpy of fusion for pure Cr and V have been collected and reviewed by Obaied et al. [] and Arblaster [], respectively. The discrepancies of the measured data from different resources have been clearly clarified by them. Therefore, the reviewed thermodynamic properties are adopted in the present modeling. In addition, the thermal vacancy concentrations in pure Cr and V at their melting temperature were experimentally investigated by means of modulation and drop methods [,]. It is generally accepted that the effects of thermal vacancy on thermodynamic properties will become obvious with the temperature above 2/3Tm []. Thus, the expressions of defect-free Gibbs energy expressions (GiA2,df) in Equation (1) of pure Cr and V in their solid stable states (below Tm) were evaluated by fitting the experimental heat capacity from 0 K to 2/3Tm.
